labashi-marduk.s: Labashi-Marduk was king of Babylon for a few months in 556 BCE, succeeding his father Neriglissar while still young. He was murdered in a conspiracy of court officials, which brought Nabonidus to the throne.

lad-khan-temple.s: The Lad Khan Temple is an early Hindu temple at Aihole in northern Karnataka, India, built under the Chalukyas of Badami, probably in the late seventh or early eighth century. Dedicated to Shiva, it has a flat roof over a square hall of pillars, modelled on timber assembly…

lado-enclave.s: The Lado Enclave was a territory on the west bank of the upper White Nile leased by Britain to Leopold II of Belgium in 1894 for his lifetime, giving the Congo Free State access to the Nile. Administered from Lado, it reverted to the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan in 1910 after his…

louis-ii-count-of-flanders.s: Louis II, known as Louis of Male, was count of Flanders from 1346 to 1384 and also count of Nevers and Rethel. He steered between England and France, won Antwerp and Mechelen from Brabant, and faced a long revolt of Ghent, which French help defeated at Roosebeke in 1382.

louis-vi-of-france.s: Louis VI, called the Fat, was king of France from 1108 to 1137. He strengthened royal authority in the Île-de-France by subduing rebellious castellans, aided by his adviser Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis.

lys-department.s: Lys was a department of the French Republic and Empire, formed in 1795 after the annexation of the Austrian Netherlands. Named after the river Lys, it covered the western part of the former County of Flanders, and its capital was Bruges.

landrecies.s: Landrecies is a small town on the Sambre in the Nord department of northern France, formerly part of the County of Hainaut. A fortified frontier town, it was besieged repeatedly in the wars between France and the Habsburgs and passed to France by the Treaty of the Pyrenees in…

le-quesnoy.s: Le Quesnoy is a small fortified town in the Nord department of northern France, formerly part of the County of Hainaut, where its counts had a castle. It passed to France by the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659 and was refortified by Vauban.

lobbes-abbey.s: Lobbes Abbey was a Benedictine monastery on the Sambre in Hainaut, in present-day Belgium, founded in the seventh century by Saint Landelin. In the tenth and eleventh centuries it was one of the leading centres of learning in Lotharingia, under abbots such as Folcuin and Heriger.

llibre-dels-fets.s: The Llibre dels fets ('Book of Deeds') is the chronicle of the reign of James I of Aragon, the Conqueror, dictated in Catalan by the king himself. Recounting his conquests of Majorca and Valencia in the first person, it is the first of the four great Catalan chronicles and one…

llotja-de-la-seda.s: The Llotja de la Seda, or Silk Exchange, in Valencia is a late Gothic merchants' exchange whose great hall of twisted columns was built in 1482–1498 under the master Pere Compte, with later wings completed by 1533. It housed the trade in silk and other goods when Valencia was…

ludvik-svoboda.s: Ludvík Svoboda was a Czechoslovak general who commanded the Czechoslovak units raised in the Soviet Union in the Second World War, including the 1st Czechoslovak Army Corps. Defence minister after 1945, he was purged in the 1950s and later rehabilitated.

life-of-columba.s: The Life of Columba is a Latin life of Saint Columba, founder of the monastery of Iona, written by Adomnán, the ninth abbot of Iona, around 700. Arranged in three books of prophecies, miracles and visions, it is the most important source for early Dál Riata, Iona and the…

league-of-armed-neutrality.s: The League of Armed Neutrality was an alliance of neutral naval powers formed to protect their shipping from British searches in wartime. The first league, organised by Catherine II of Russia in 1780 with Denmark-Norway and Sweden and later joined by the Dutch Republic and…

ludvig-holberg.s: Ludvig Holberg was a writer and historian born in Bergen, Norway, who spent his career as a professor at the University of Copenhagen. His comedies, such as Jeppe of the Hill and Erasmus Montanus, his satirical novel Niels Klim and his histories founded modern literature in…

la-rochelle.s: La Rochelle is a port city on the Atlantic coast of western France, in the old province of Aunis. In the Middle Ages it exported wine and salt to northern Europe and passed between the English and French crowns, falling to Louis VIII in 1224.

libourne.s: Libourne is a town in the Gironde department of south-western France, where the Isle meets the Dordogne. It was founded as a bastide around 1270 by Roger of Leybourne, seneschal of Gascony for the future Edward I, and named after him.

luitpoldings.s: The Luitpoldings were a Bavarian noble dynasty that ruled the Duchy of Bavaria in the late ninth and tenth centuries. Its founder, Margrave Luitpold, fell fighting the Magyars at Pressburg in 907, and his son Arnulf made Bavaria a powerful stem duchy within East Francia.

la-brabanconne.s: La Brabançonne is the national anthem of Belgium, written during the Belgian Revolution of 1830 with words by Jenneval, a French actor in Brussels, and music by François Van Campenhout. Its name recalls Brabant, the old duchy at whose heart Brussels lies.

lier-belgium.s: Lier is a city in the province of Antwerp, Belgium, where the Grote and Kleine Nete rivers meet. A cloth-making town of the Duchy of Brabant in the Middle Ages, it was where Philip the Handsome married Joanna of Castile in 1496.

langeais.s: Langeais is a small town on the Loire in the Indre-et-Loire department of central France, west of Tours. It has the ruins of one of the oldest stone keeps in France, built by Fulk Nerra in the late tenth century, and a castle rebuilt for Louis XI in the 1460s.

league-of-the-public-weal.s: The League of the Public Weal was an alliance of great French nobles formed in 1465 against Louis XI, led by Charles of Charolais (later Charles the Bold), Duke Francis II of Brittany, Duke John II of Bourbon and the king's brother Charles of Berry. After the indecisive Battle…

louis-ii-de-la-tremoille.s: Louis II de La Trémoille was a French commander who served Charles VIII, Louis XII and Francis I. In 1488 he defeated the Breton army at Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier, and he later fought in the Italian Wars at Fornovo, Agnadello and Marignano.

lower-brittany.s: Lower Brittany (Basse-Bretagne) is the western half of Brittany, where the Breton language was traditionally spoken, in contrast to Upper Brittany in the east, where Gallo and French prevailed. It covers roughly Finistère and the western parts of the Côtes-d'Armor and Morbihan.

la-mothe-en-bassigny.s: La Mothe-en-Bassigny was a fortified town on a hilltop in the Bassigny, on the south-western border of the Duchy of Lorraine, in today's Haute-Marne department. A key ducal stronghold, it was besieged several times by the French during the Thirty Years' War.

luneville.s: Lunéville is a town on the Meurthe in the Meurthe-et-Moselle department of north-eastern France. Duke Leopold of Lorraine built a large palace there from 1703, inspired by Versailles, and it remained the court of the dukes and then of Stanisław Leszczyński until 1766.

les-andelys.s: Les Andelys is a town on the Seine in the Eure department of Normandy. Above it stands Château Gaillard, built by Richard the Lionheart in 1196–1198 to defend Normandy against Philip II of France and taken by the French in 1204 after a long siege.

louise-marie-therese-of-artois.s: Louise Marie Thérèse of Artois was a granddaughter of Charles X of France and the wife of Charles III, duke of Parma. After her husband's assassination in 1854 she governed the duchy as regent for their young son Robert I.

lake-geneva.s: Lake Geneva is a large lake on the north side of the Alps, shared between Switzerland and France, through which the Rhône flows. Geneva lies at its south-western end and Lausanne on its northern shore.

liutgard-of-saxony.s: Liutgard of Saxony was a daughter of Count Liudolf, founder of the Liudolfing dynasty, and his wife Oda, who founded the convent of Gandersheim. In the 870s she married the Carolingian king Louis the Younger of East Francia, a match that showed the rising standing of her family.

linggadjati-agreement.s: The Linggadjati Agreement was a settlement negotiated in November 1946 at Linggadjati near Cirebon in West Java between the Netherlands and the Republic of Indonesia, and signed in March 1947. The Dutch recognised the Republic's de facto authority over Java, Madura and…

lama-dorji.s: Lama Dorji was ruler of the Dzungar Khanate from 1750 to 1753, a son of Galdan Tseren by a lesser wife. In 1750 he overthrew and blinded his half-brother, the young khan Tsewang Dorji Namjal.

langya-commandery.s: Langya was a commandery of early imperial China in the south-east of present-day Shandong. Sima Rui held the title Prince of Langya before founding the Eastern Jin dynasty in 317, and the Wang clan of Langya, who followed him south of the Yangtze, became the most powerful…

liu-laozhi.s: Liu Laozhi was a general of the Eastern Jin dynasty and commander of the Beifu army based at Jingkou. He fought at the Battle of Fei River in 383 and against the rebel Sun En, and by changing sides he decided several struggles at court.

lu-xun.s: Lu Xun, the pen name of Zhou Shuren, was a Chinese writer regarded as the founder of modern Chinese literature. His short stories in the vernacular, such as 'A Madman's Diary' (1918) and 'The True Story of Ah Q', attacked the traditions he blamed for China's weakness and made…

lu-xun-rebel.s: Lu Xun was a Daoist rebel leader of the Eastern Jin period and brother-in-law of Sun En. After Sun En's death in 402 he led the remnants of the rebellion, took Guangzhou and held the far south, and in 410, while Liu Yu was campaigning against the Southern Yan, he advanced…

lantingji-xu.s: The Lantingji Xu (Preface to the Poems Composed at the Orchid Pavilion) is a short prose text written by Wang Xizhi in 353 for a collection of poems composed by his friends at a spring gathering at the Orchid Pavilion near Shaoxing. Regarded as the most celebrated work of…

lower-rhine.s: The Lower Rhine is the section of the Rhine below Bonn, where the river leaves the Rhenish Massif and flows across the North German Plain through North Rhine-Westphalia to the Netherlands; the name also denotes the surrounding region. Cologne, Düsseldorf and Duisburg lie along…

louis-i-duke-of-bavaria.s: Louis I, called the Kelheimer, was Duke of Bavaria of the house of Wittelsbach from 1183 to 1231. In 1214 Emperor Frederick II granted him the Palatinate of the Rhine, which his family secured by marrying his son Otto II to the Welf heiress Agnes, beginning nearly six…

laz-people.s: The Laz are a Kartvelian-speaking people of the south-eastern Black Sea coast, living mainly in north-eastern Turkey around Rize and Artvin and in Adjara in Georgia. Descended from the ancient Colchians, they gave their name to the late antique kingdom of Lazica.

leleges.s: The Leleges were a people named by Greek writers as early inhabitants of the Aegean coasts and islands, especially Caria, Ionia and parts of mainland Greece, before Greek settlement. Ancient authors often linked them with the Carians, and their identity, language and origins…

livingston-codes.s: The Livingston Codes were penal and procedural codes drafted by the American jurist Edward Livingston for Louisiana and adopted in the State of Guatemala in the 1830s under the liberal head of state Mariano Gálvez. They introduced trial by jury and other reforms modelled on…

lake-prespa.s: Lake Prespa is a pair of lakes in the mountains of the southern Balkans, shared by North Macedonia, Albania and Greece. Around 1000 Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria made it a centre of his realm, building a basilica and residence on the island of Saint Achillius in Small Prespa Lake,…

louis-nicolas-davout.s: Louis-Nicolas Davout (1770–1823) was one of Napoleon's ablest marshals, victor over the Prussians at Auerstedt in 1806 and created Duke of Auerstedt and Prince of Eckmühl. As governor of Hamburg in 1813–1814 he held the city against a Russian-led siege, expelling thousands of…

long-recess.s: The Long Recess (Langer Rezess) of 1529 was an agreement between the council and citizens of Hamburg concluded with the introduction of the Reformation. It gave the propertied citizens, organised by parish, a share in government beside the council, including a say over…

ludwig-roselius.s: Ludwig Roselius (1874–1943) was a Bremen coffee merchant who founded Kaffee HAG in 1906 to sell the first commercially successful decaffeinated coffee, using a process he had patented. He also financed the Böttcherstrasse in Bremen, a street of Expressionist buildings built in…

louis-de-bourmont.s: Louis de Bourmont (1773–1846) was a French general and royalist who had fought in the Vendée revolt before serving Napoleon, whom he deserted on the eve of Waterloo. As minister of war under Charles X, he led the expedition that captured Algiers in July 1830 and was made a…

loi-cadre-defferre.s: The Loi Cadre Defferre was a French framework law of 23 June 1956, named after the overseas minister Gaston Defferre, that reformed the government of France's African and Malagasy territories. It introduced universal suffrage on a single electoral roll and gave each territory…

li-shiji.s: Li Shiji, often called Li Ji, was one of the leading generals of the early Tang dynasty in China. He took part in the destruction of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate in 630 and served the emperors Taizong and Gaozong for decades.

louis-iii-grand-duke-of-hesse.n: Louis III, Grand Duke of Hesse
louis-iii-grand-duke-of-hesse.s: Louis III was grand duke of Hesse from 1848 to 1877, succeeding his father Louis II during the revolution. His reign saw the conservative government of Reinhard von Dalwigk, defeat as Austria's ally in 1866 and entry into the German Empire in 1871.

lithuanian-metrica.s: The Lithuanian Metrica is the archive of the chancery of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, consisting of copybooks of charters, court decisions, treaties and other records from the fifteenth to the eighteenth century. Most entries are in Ruthenian, with later ones in Latin and…

luxembourg-crisis.s: The Luxembourg Crisis of 1867 was a diplomatic confrontation between France and Prussia over the status of Luxembourg. Napoleon III negotiated to buy the grand duchy from William III of the Netherlands, but Prussian and German opposition raised the threat of war.

luxembourgers.s: Luxembourgers are the people and citizens of Luxembourg, a small nation whose national identity developed after the grand duchy became independent in the nineteenth century. Their national language is Luxembourgish, used alongside French and German, and their motto, 'We want…

luxembourgish.s: Luxembourgish is a West Germanic language, derived from Moselle Franconian dialects, spoken as a mother tongue by most Luxembourgers. Long regarded as a German dialect, it became a symbol of national identity during and after the German occupation of the Second World War, and…

luxleaks.s: LuxLeaks was a financial scandal revealed in November 2014 by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. Leaked documents from the accounting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers showed that Luxembourg's tax authorities had approved hundreds of advance tax rulings…

leopold-ii-grand-duke-of-tuscany.n: Leopold II, Grand Duke of Tuscany
leopold-ii-grand-duke-of-tuscany.s: Leopold II was the last reigning Grand Duke of Tuscany of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine, ruling from 1824 to 1859. His early reign was mild and reforming, with drainage of the Maremma and a relatively free press, but after the revolutions of 1848–1849 he returned under…

leopoldo-de-medici.s: Leopoldo de' Medici was a prince of the Tuscan ruling house, brother of Grand Duke Ferdinando II, and a cardinal from 1667. A keen student of science, he founded the Accademia del Cimento with his brother in 1657 and directed its experiments.

las-meninas.s: Las Meninas is a painting by Diego Velázquez, completed in 1656 and now in the Prado in Madrid. It shows the Infanta Margarita Teresa with her maids of honour and attendants in the painter's studio, with Velázquez himself at his easel and the king and queen reflected in a mirror.

luis-de-gongora.s: Luis de Góngora was a Spanish poet of the Golden Age from Córdoba. His Soledades and Fable of Polyphemus and Galatea, with their Latinate syntax, learned allusions and dense metaphors, created the style called culteranismo or Gongorism, which provoked fierce controversy,…

louis-grand-conde.s: Louis, Grand Condé, born Louis II de Bourbon and Prince of Condé from 1646, was one of the leading French generals of the seventeenth century. As the young Duke of Enghien he destroyed the Spanish army at Rocroi in 1643, and he won further victories in the Thirty Years' War.

louis-de-buade-de-frontenac.s: Louis de Buade de Frontenac was a French soldier who served twice as governor general of New France, from 1672 to 1682 and from 1689 to 1698. He expanded the fur trade westward and built Fort Frontenac on Lake Ontario in 1673.

lachine-massacre.s: The Lachine massacre was a surprise attack by about 1,500 Iroquois warriors on the French settlement of Lachine, on the island of Montreal, on 5 August 1689. Dozens of settlers were killed and many more taken captive, and the raid spread terror across New France.

lake-champlain.s: Lake Champlain is a long, narrow lake between New York and Vermont that extends north into Quebec and drains into the St Lawrence through the Richelieu River. It is named after Samuel de Champlain, who reached it in 1609 and fought the Mohawk on its shores.

liu-wansu.s: Liu Wansu was a physician of the Jin dynasty from Hejian in Hebei and one of the four great medical masters of the Jin and Yuan periods. He argued that many diseases arose from excessive heat or fire, and treated them with cooling and purging drugs, founding what became known…

lugou-bridge.s: The Lugou Bridge, known in the West as the Marco Polo Bridge, is a granite bridge of eleven arches over the Yongding River south-west of Beijing, built under the Jin dynasty between 1189 and 1192. Its balustrades carry hundreds of carved stone lions, and Marco Polo described…

leele-fuli-fak.s: Leele Fuli Fak was a buurba, or ruler, of the Jolof Empire in present-day Senegal in the mid-sixteenth century, the last to rule it while it still held the coastal kingdoms. Around 1549 he was defeated and killed at the Battle of Danki by the forces of Amari Ngone Sobel Fall…

lake-katwe.s: Lake Katwe is a salt lake in a volcanic crater in western Uganda, north of Lake Edward, within what is now Queen Elizabeth National Park. Salt has been worked there for centuries and was traded widely across the Great Lakes region, reaching kingdoms such as Nkore, Bunyoro and…

lerins-abbey.s: Lérins Abbey is a monastery on the island of Saint-Honorat off Cannes, founded around 410 by Saint Honoratus. In the fifth and sixth centuries it was one of the most influential monastic centres of the West, training bishops and writers such as Vincent of Lérins, Hilary of…

liutprand-of-cremona.s: Liutprand of Cremona was a Lombard historian, diplomat and bishop of Cremona from 961. After serving King Berengar II of Italy he joined Otto I, who sent him on embassies to Constantinople.

lothair-ii-of-italy.s: Lothair II was king of Italy, a son of Hugh of Arles, who made him co-king in 931; he ruled alone from 947 until his early death in 950. He married Adelaide, daughter of Rudolf II of Burgundy, and after his death Berengar of Ivrea seized the throne.

lower-burgundy.s: Lower Burgundy, or the Kingdom of Provence, was the kingdom founded in 879 when Boso of Vienne was elected king at Mantaille, covering the Rhône valley and Provence. His son Louis the Blind was crowned emperor in 901 but blinded in 905, and real power passed to Hugh of Arles.

lake-starnberg.s: Lake Starnberg is a lake south-west of Munich, about 20 kilometres long, long favoured by the Bavarian court and the city's wealthy for summer residences. On 13 June 1886, days after he had been declared unfit to rule, Ludwig II of Bavaria was found dead in its shallow waters…

leo-von-klenze.s: Leo von Klenze was a German neoclassical architect and court architect of Ludwig I of Bavaria. In Munich he built the Glyptothek, the Alte Pinakothek, the Ruhmeshalle and much of the Ludwigstrasse, and near Regensburg the Walhalla, a Greek-style temple of German worthies.

leopold-von-ranke.s: Leopold von Ranke was a German historian and a founder of modern source-based history. Teaching at Berlin, he insisted on the critical study of original documents to show the past "as it actually was", and wrote major histories of the popes, the Reformation and the European…

ludwig-canal.s: The Ludwig Canal was a waterway linking the Main at Bamberg with the Danube at Kelheim, built between 1836 and 1846 on the orders of Ludwig I of Bavaria. About 170 kilometres long with around a hundred locks, it connected the Rhine and Danube river systems.

ludwig-railway.s: The Ludwig Railway was the first railway in Germany worked by steam locomotives, opened on 7 December 1835 between Nuremberg and Fürth, a distance of about 6 kilometres. Named after Ludwig I of Bavaria, it was built by a private company, and its first locomotive, the Adler,…

ludwigstrasse.s: The Ludwigstrasse is a monumental avenue in Munich, laid out for Ludwig I of Bavaria from 1816, running north from the Odeonsplatz and the Feldherrnhalle to the Siegestor. Its southern part was designed by Leo von Klenze and its northern part by Friedrich von Gärtner, who…

la-muette-de-portici.s: La Muette de Portici is a French grand opera by Daniel Auber, first performed in Paris in 1828. Set during the Neapolitan revolt of Masaniello against Spanish rule in 1647, it includes the patriotic duet "Amour sacré de la patrie".

land-ordinance-of-vladislaus-ii.s: The Land Ordinance of Vladislaus II was a code of the land law of the Kingdom of Bohemia, issued in 1500 under King Vladislaus II Jagiellon. Drawn up by the estates, it confirmed the dominance of the lords and knights in the diet and the courts and restricted the political…

letter-of-majesty.s: The Letter of Majesty was a charter issued in July 1609 by Rudolf II, as king of Bohemia, under pressure from the Protestant estates. It guaranteed freedom of religion to Protestants and Utraquists and allowed them to build churches and schools, with defenders elected to…

lusatia.s: Lusatia is a historical region in Central Europe between the Elbe and the Oder, divided into Upper and Lower Lusatia and today split between Germany and Poland. It is the home of the Sorbs, a Slavic people.

luganda.s: Luganda is the Bantu language of the Baganda of central Uganda. It is spoken as a first language by several million people and as a second language by many more, making it the most widely spoken indigenous language of Uganda.

lukiiko.s: The Lukiiko is the council or parliament of the Kingdom of Buganda. Originally an assembly of chiefs that advised the kabaka and heard important cases, it was recognised as the kingdom's legislature by the Buganda Agreement of 1900.

lango.s: Lango is a region of northern Uganda north of Lake Kyoga, home of the Lango people, who speak a Luo language. In the nineteenth century it lay beyond the borders of the kingdoms and served as a refuge for Kabalega during his war against the British; he and Mwanga II were…

luo-peoples.s: The Luo are a group of Nilotic peoples who spread from the region of the southern Sudan into present-day Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of the Congo from around the fifteenth century. They include the Acholi, Alur, Lango and Kenya Luo.

lund.s: Lund is a city in Scania, southern Sweden, founded by Danish kings around 990. It became a seat of bishops and, in 1103 or 1104, the archbishopric of all Scandinavia, and its Romanesque cathedral was consecrated in 1145.

london-conference-of-1832.s: The London Conference of 1832 was a meeting of Britain, France and Russia that settled the form of the new Kingdom of Greece. The powers chose Otto, the son of Ludwig I of Bavaria, as king and guaranteed a loan to the new state.

llangadwaladr.s: Llangadwaladr is a small village in south-west Anglesey, Wales, near the royal court of Aberffraw. Its church, dedicated to Cadwaladr, holds the Cadfan Stone, a seventh-century inscribed memorial in Latin to Cadfan ap Iago, king of Gwynedd, describing him as the wisest and…

llyfr-iorwerth.s: Llyfr Iorwerth, the Book of Iorwerth, is the Gwynedd version of the medieval Welsh laws attributed to Hywel Dda, compiled in the thirteenth century and associated with the jurist Iorwerth ap Madog. Written in Welsh, it is the fullest and most developed of the Welsh law texts,…

llys-rhosyr.s: Llys Rhosyr is the site of a medieval royal court of the princes of Gwynedd near Newborough in south-west Anglesey, Wales. Excavations from 1992 uncovered the stone foundations of its halls and enclosure wall, the only such court of the Welsh princes to have been excavated.

llywarch-ap-llywelyn.s: Llywarch ap Llywelyn, known as Prydydd y Moch ('Poet of the Pigs'), was one of the leading Poets of the Princes in medieval Wales, active from about 1173 to 1220. He composed elaborate praise poems for the rulers of Gwynedd, above all Llywelyn the Great, whose rise he celebrated.

lower-austria.s: Lower Austria is the largest state of Austria, lying in the north-east of the country around Vienna, which was long its capital; St. Pölten replaced it in 1986.

luigi-cadorna.s: Luigi Cadorna was chief of staff of the Italian army from 1914 to 1917. He launched eleven costly offensives on the Isonzo front and imposed harsh discipline, including summary executions.

libnah.s: Libnah was a town in the Shephelah of Judah, often identified with Tel Burna near Kiryat Gat, although its location is uncertain. According to 2 Kings it revolted against King Jehoram in the 9th century BCE, and in 701 BCE Sennacherib attacked it after taking Lachish.

leofric-earl-of-mercia.s: Leofric was Earl of Mercia from about 1030 until his death in 1057, one of the three great earls of England under Cnut and Edward the Confessor alongside Godwin and Siward. He often acted as a mediator in the political crises of Edward's reign.

lalbagh-botanical-garden.s: Lalbagh Botanical Garden is a historic garden in Bengaluru (Bangalore), India. It was begun by Hyder Ali around 1760 on the Mughal garden model and enlarged by his son Tipu Sultan, who brought in plants from many lands.

luca-giordano.s: Luca Giordano (1634–1705) was a Neapolitan Baroque painter, nicknamed Fa Presto for the speed of his work. Influenced by Ribera and the Venetians, he painted large altarpieces and fresco cycles across Italy, including the ceiling of the Palazzo Medici Riccardi in Florence, and…

ley-paccionada.s: The Ley Paccionada is the Spanish law of 16 August 1841 that ended the Kingdom of Navarre's status as a separate realm after the First Carlist War. Negotiated between Navarre's representatives and the government in Madrid, it made Navarre a province of Spain while preserving…

lanse-aux-meadows.s: L'Anse aux Meadows is an archaeological site at the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada, the only confirmed Norse settlement in North America. Discovered in 1960 by Helge Ingstad and excavated with Anne Stine Ingstad, it contained the remains of turf buildings occupied…

laodice-vi.s: Laodice VI was a Seleucid princess, daughter of Antiochus IV, who married Mithridates V of Pontus. After his assassination around 120 BCE she ruled Pontus as regent for her young sons, apparently favouring the younger.

lex-manilia.s: The Lex Manilia was a Roman law proposed by the tribune Gaius Manilius in 66 BCE that gave Pompey command of the war against Mithridates VI of Pontus and Tigranes of Armenia, with very wide powers in the east. Cicero spoke in its favour in his speech De imperio Cn.

lucius-licinius-murena.s: Lucius Licinius Murena was a Roman commander who served under Sulla in the First Mithridatic War and was left as governor of Asia. In 83 BCE he attacked Pontus without clear authority, starting the Second Mithridatic War, and was defeated by Mithridates VI in 82 BCE.

leiria.s: Leiria is a city in central Portugal, between Lisbon and Coimbra. Afonso Henriques took it from the Moors and built its castle in 1135, and it became a royal residence.

lines-of-torres-vedras.s: The Lines of Torres Vedras were lines of forts and earthworks built in secret in 1809–1810 on Wellington's orders to defend Lisbon during the Peninsular War. Stretching across the peninsula north of the city, they stopped Marshal Masséna's French army in October 1810.

luis-de-camoes.s: Luís Vaz de Camões was Portugal's greatest poet. He lost an eye fighting in Morocco and spent many years as a soldier and official in India and the Far East before returning to Lisbon, where his epic Os Lusíadas was published in 1572.

landwehr.s: The Landwehr was a militia of men outside the regular army, best known in Prussia, where it was raised in 1813 for the war of liberation against Napoleon as part of the military reforms of Scharnhorst and Gneisenau. It fought at Leipzig and Waterloo.

landtag-of-prussia.s: The Landtag of Prussia was the parliament of the Kingdom of Prussia and later the Free State of Prussia. Under the constitution of 1850 it had an elected House of Representatives, chosen by a three-class franchise weighted by taxes paid, and an appointed House of Lords, which…

lake-kivu.s: Lake Kivu is one of the African Great Lakes, in the Albertine Rift on the border between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It drains south through the Ruzizi river into Lake Tanganyika, and its deep waters hold large amounts of dissolved methane.

leonardo-alagon.s: Leonardo Alagon was Marquis of Oristano, heir through his mother to the old Judicate of Arborea in Sardinia. Quarrelling with the Aragonese viceroy, he rose in revolt in the 1470s and won early successes, but was defeated at the Battle of Macomer in 1478.

lords-of-the-articles.s: The Lords of the Articles was a standing committee of the Parliament of Scotland, drawn from its estates, which prepared the legislation that the full parliament then approved. It appeared in the later fourteenth century and under the Stuart kings became a means of royal…

leviathan.s: Leviathan is a sea monster of the Hebrew Bible, described in the Psalms, Isaiah and the Book of Job as a serpent or dragon of the sea overcome by God. The figure derives from older Canaanite tradition: Ugaritic texts of the Late Bronze Age tell of the defeat of Lotan, a…

lotan.s: Lotan is a seven-headed sea serpent in the Ugaritic texts of the Late Bronze Age, called the fleeing serpent and the twisting serpent, and defeated by the storm god Baal and the goddess Anat. A servant of the sea god Yam, it embodies the forces of chaos that the storm god…

ludwig-uhland.s: Ludwig Uhland was a German poet, literary scholar and liberal politician from Tübingen, the leading figure of the Swabian school of poets. His ballads and songs, such as Der gute Kamerad, became widely popular.

little-entente.s: The Little Entente was an alliance formed in 1920–1921 by Czechoslovakia, Romania and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, with the backing of France. Its aim was to prevent Hungarian revision of the post-war frontiers and a Habsburg restoration and to defend the…

louis-barthou.s: Louis Barthou was a French politician who was prime minister in 1913 and foreign minister in 1934. He sought to contain Nazi Germany through alliances in Eastern Europe, including with the Soviet Union, and was killed on 9 October 1934 in Marseille during the assassination of…

luanda-island.s: Luanda Island, or Ilha de Luanda, is a narrow sandy strip, originally an island, off the coast of Luanda, the capital of Angola. In the time of the Kingdom of Kongo it was a royal fishery where the nzimbu shells used as the kingdom's currency were gathered under the king's…

lokaksema.s: Lokaksema was a Buddhist monk from the Kushan lands who worked in the Chinese capital Luoyang in the 170s and 180s CE. He made some of the earliest Chinese translations of Mahayana sutras, among them a version of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, and his work…

le-duy-mat.s: Lê Duy Mật was a prince of the Later Lê dynasty who rebelled against the Trịnh lords, the real rulers of northern Vietnam. From 1738 he fought for three decades, holding a base in the mountains of Trấn Ninh, until Trịnh forces took his stronghold in 1770 and he died.

le-hien-tong.s: Lê Hiến Tông was emperor of Vietnam of the Later Lê dynasty from 1497 to 1504. The son of Lê Thánh Tông, he preserved his father's Confucian institutions and examination system, and his reign is counted as the last of the dynasty's stable period before decades of misrule and…

le-nghi-dan.s: Lê Nghi Dân was the eldest son of the emperor Lê Thái Tông. Passed over for the succession, he seized the throne in 1459 by killing his half-brother Lê Nhân Tông, but his rule lasted only eight months before court officials overthrew and killed him and enthroned Lê Thánh Tông.

le-nhan-tong.s: Lê Nhân Tông was emperor of Vietnam of the Later Lê dynasty from 1442 to 1459. He came to the throne as an infant, and his mother governed as regent until 1453.

le-quy-don.s: Lê Quý Đôn was a Vietnamese scholar-official of the late Lê period, often regarded as the most learned man of his age. He wrote encyclopaedic works on history, geography, administration and natural knowledge, including the Phủ biên tạp lục, a survey of the southern frontier,…

le-thai-tong.s: Lê Thái Tông was emperor of Vietnam of the Later Lê dynasty from 1433 to 1442, succeeding his father Lê Lợi as a boy. He died suddenly in 1442 after visiting the estate of the scholar Nguyễn Trãi, who was blamed and executed with his family, a case later recognised as an…

le-trang-tong.s: Lê Trang Tông was emperor of Vietnam from 1533 to 1548, the first ruler of the restored Later Lê line. Enthroned in exile by the loyalist general Nguyễn Kim, who opposed the Mạc dynasty, he reigned in the hills of Laos and Thanh Hóa while real power passed to Nguyễn Kim and…

le-tuong-duc.s: Lê Tương Dực was emperor of Vietnam of the Later Lê dynasty from 1510 to 1516. He took the throne by overthrowing Lê Uy Mục, but his costly palace building and heavy labour demands provoked rebellions, including that of Trần Cảo, and he was killed by one of his own generals in…

le-uy-muc.s: Lê Uy Mục was emperor of Vietnam of the Later Lê dynasty from 1505 to 1509, remembered as a cruel and dissolute ruler. He purged members of the royal family and officials, and was overthrown and killed in 1509 by his cousin, who reigned as Lê Tương Dực.

liu-sheng-ming-general.s: Liu Sheng was a general of the Ming dynasty who commanded the relief army sent in 1427 to rescue the Ming garrison besieged by Lê Lợi in Vietnam. Ambushed at the Chi Lăng pass, he was killed and his army destroyed, a defeat that led the Ming to abandon their occupation of Đại…

leymah-gbowee.s: Leymah Gbowee is a Liberian peace activist who led the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace, a movement of Christian and Muslim women whose protests helped bring an end to the Second Liberian Civil War in 2003. She shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011 with Ellen Johnson…

loma-people.s: The Loma are a Mande-speaking people of north-western Liberia, mainly in Lofa County, and of neighbouring Guinea, where they are called Toma. They farm rice in the forest highlands, and the Poro society is central to their social and religious life.

liberians-united-for-reconciliation-and-.n: Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy
liberians-united-for-reconciliation-and-.s: Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy (LURD) was a rebel movement that fought the government of Charles Taylor from 1999, beginning the Second Liberian Civil War. Backed by Guinea, it advanced on Monrovia in 2003, and with the MODEL rebels forced Taylor to resign…

lueji.s: Lueji (Rweej) is the legendary queen of the Lunda of central Africa, heiress of a Lunda ruling line on the upper Kasai. According to Lunda oral tradition she married the Luba hunter-prince Chibinda Ilunga, who brought the Luba model of sacred kingship, and their line founded…

lukonkesh.s: Lukonkesh (Lukokesha) was the title of the queen mother of the Lunda Empire in central Africa, a female dignitary of high rank at the royal capital, the musumba. Regarded as the symbolic mother of the Mwaant Yaav, she held her own court and lands and took part in the council…

lake-nasser.s: Lake Nasser is a reservoir on the Nile in southern Egypt and northern Sudan, created by the Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970. More than 500 kilometres long, it flooded much of Lower Nubia, displacing about 100,000 Nubians and prompting the UNESCO campaign that moved Abu…

lahad-datu.s: Lahad Datu is a town on the east coast of Sabah in Malaysian Borneo, a centre of the palm-oil industry. In February 2013 more than 200 armed followers of Jamalul Kiram III, a claimant to the Sultanate of Sulu, landed nearby to press the sultanate's historic claim to Sabah, and…

look-east-policy.s: The Look East Policy was an economic and educational policy launched by the Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad in 1982. It urged Malaysians to learn from the work ethic, management and industrial methods of Japan and South Korea rather than the West, and sent thousands…

lehnin-abbey.s: Lehnin Abbey is a former Cistercian monastery in Brandenburg, Germany, founded in 1180 by Margrave Otto I, son of Albert the Bear. One of the oldest monasteries in the Mark, it was a burial place of the Ascanian margraves and a centre of German settlement and land clearance.

louis-v-duke-of-bavaria.s: Louis V, called Louis the Brandenburger, was Margrave of Brandenburg from 1323 to 1351 and later Duke of Upper Bavaria. The eldest son of Emperor Louis IV of the House of Wittelsbach, he received Brandenburg after the Ascanian line died out, but his rule was shaken by the…

lands-of-the-bohemian-crown.s: The Lands of the Bohemian Crown were the territories united under the kings of Bohemia: the Kingdom of Bohemia, the Margraviate of Moravia, Silesia and, for long periods, Upper and Lower Lusatia. Charles IV defined them as a single union under the Crown of Bohemia in 1348.

lennart-torstensson.s: Lennart Torstensson was a Swedish field marshal and artillery commander in the Thirty Years' War. Commander of the Swedish army in Germany from 1641, he won the Second Battle of Breitenfeld in 1642 and the Battle of Jankau in 1645, then advanced towards Vienna but failed to…

leos-janacek.s: Leoš Janáček was a Czech composer, born at Hukvaldy in Moravia, who spent most of his career in Brno, where he founded an organ school. Drawing on Moravian folk music and the rhythms of Czech speech, he wrote operas such as Jenůfa, Káťa Kabanová and The Cunning Little Vixen,…

lasem.s: Lasem is a coastal town in Rembang Regency, Central Java, on the north coast of Java. A port and seat of local rulers in the Majapahit period and after, it was conquered by Sultan Agung of Mataram in 1616.

lion-capital-of-ashoka.s: The Lion Capital of Ashoka is a polished sandstone sculpture of four lions standing back to back, which crowned a pillar erected by the Maurya emperor Ashoka at Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon. Made around 250 BCE, it was excavated in 1905 and is kept in the…

luis-donaldo-colosio.s: Luis Donaldo Colosio was a Mexican politician and the presidential candidate of the Institutional Revolutionary Party in 1994. A former party president and minister of social development, he was shot dead at a campaign rally in Tijuana on 23 March 1994.

leon-trotsky.s: Leon Trotsky was a Russian Marxist revolutionary who organised the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917 with Lenin. As People's Commissar for War from 1918 he built the Red Army and led it to victory in the Russian Civil War.

liberation-army-of-the-south.s: The Liberation Army of the South was the revolutionary army of Emiliano Zapata, drawn mainly from the peasants of Morelos, which fought from 1911 for the return of village lands under the Plan of Ayala. It opposed Madero, Huerta and Carranza in turn.

loyalist-instruction.s: The Loyalist Instruction is an ancient Egyptian teaching text of the Middle Kingdom, known from the stele of the official Sehetepibre and from later papyri. It urges loyalty to the king, presenting him as the source of life and prosperity, and then turns to the proper…

little-ice-age.s: The Little Ice Age was a period of cooler climate, especially in the Northern Hemisphere, between roughly the 14th and mid-19th centuries, with particularly cold phases in the 17th century. Advancing glaciers, shorter growing seasons and harvest failures contributed to famine,…

lake-huron.s: Lake Huron is the second largest of the Great Lakes of North America by area, lying between Ontario in Canada and Michigan in the United States. It was named by the French after the Huron, or Wendat, who lived near Georgian Bay, and Samuel de Champlain reached its shores in 1615.

louis-joseph-de-montcalm.s: Louis-Joseph de Montcalm was a French general who commanded the French army in North America during the Seven Years' War from 1756. He took Fort Oswego in 1756 and Fort William Henry in 1757 and won a notable defensive victory at Carillon in 1758.

laurens-de-graaf.s: Laurens de Graaf was a Dutch buccaneer who operated from French Saint-Domingue and raided Spanish shipping and ports in the Caribbean. In May 1683, with Nicholas van Hoorn and Michel de Grammont, he sacked Veracruz, the chief port of New Spain, holding its inhabitants for ransom.

le-van-khoi.s: Lê Văn Khôi was a Vietnamese officer, the adopted son of the southern governor Lê Văn Duyệt, who led a revolt against Emperor Minh Mạng in 1833. Supported by Catholics, Chinese settlers and former followers of Duyệt, he seized the Saigon citadel and sought help from Siam.

leptis-minor.s: Leptis Minor was an ancient Phoenician port on the Sahel coast of present-day Tunisia, at modern Lamta, south of Monastir. One of the rich coastal towns known as the Emporia, it was seized from Carthage by Masinissa around 161 BCE.

libyco-berber-script.s: The Libyco-Berber script is an ancient alphabet of consonants used to write Berber languages across North Africa and the Canary Islands from at least the third century BCE. It is known from thousands of funerary and rock inscriptions, and bilingual Punic texts from Dougga,…

lucius-calpurnius-piso-the-pontifex.s: Lucius Calpurnius Piso the Pontifex was a Roman senator and general, consul in 15 BCE. From about 13 to 11 BCE he fought a hard campaign in Thrace against the Bessi and other tribes who had risen against the Roman client king Rhoemetalces I, for which he received triumphal…

landsknecht.s: The Landsknechte were German mercenary soldiers, mainly pikemen, first raised around 1486 under Maximilian I of Habsburg in imitation of the Swiss infantry. They became the chief rivals of Swiss mercenaries and fought for many powers in the Italian Wars and other conflicts of…

lake-ageri.s: Lake Ägeri is a lake in the canton of Zug, central Switzerland, near the border with Schwyz. On the narrow ground between its shore and the slopes of Morgarten the men of Schwyz ambushed and defeated a Habsburg army in November 1315, one of the founding victories of the Swiss…

leonhard-euler.s: Leonhard Euler was a Swiss mathematician and physicist from Basel, one of the most prolific and influential mathematicians in history. Working at the academies of St Petersburg and Berlin, he made fundamental contributions to analysis, number theory, mechanics and the…

louw-wepener.s: Louw Wepener was a Boer commandant of the Orange Free State. Born in the Cape Colony, he led Free State burghers in the war of 1865 against Moshoeshoe's Basotho and was killed in August 1865 while leading an assault on the mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu.

leo-iv-the-khazar.s: Leo IV the Khazar was Byzantine emperor from 775 to 780, the son of Constantine V and the Khazar princess Tzitzak, from whom he took his byname. He continued his father's iconoclast policy in a milder form and fought the Abbasids in Asia Minor.

leonine-wall.s: The Leonine Wall is a defensive wall built around the Vatican hill and Saint Peter's Basilica by Pope Leo IV between 848 and 852, after Muslim raiders sacked the basilica in 846. The enclosed district became known as the Leonine City.

lorenzo-valla.s: Lorenzo Valla was an Italian humanist, rhetorician and scholar. In 1440, while serving Alfonso V of Aragon at Naples, he proved by linguistic and historical analysis that the Donation of Constantine was a forgery.

liaoshen-campaign.s: The Liaoshen campaign was the first of the three great campaigns of the Chinese Civil War, fought in Manchuria from September to November 1948. Communist forces under Lin Biao took Jinzhou, cutting off the Nationalist armies in the north-east, and then captured Changchun and…

liu-shaoqi.s: Liu Shaoqi was a leading Chinese Communist and chairman (head of state) of the People's Republic of China from 1959 to 1968. With Deng Xiaoping he led the economic recovery after the Great Leap Forward, but during the Cultural Revolution he was denounced as a capitalist…

liege-revolution.s: The Liège Revolution began in August 1789, when citizens drove out Prince-Bishop Hoensbroeck, installed new magistrates and later proclaimed a republic. It was suppressed by Austrian troops in January 1791, but the French revolutionary armies returned in 1792 and 1794, and the…

louis-de-bourbon-bishop-of-liege.s: Louis de Bourbon was prince-bishop of Liège from 1456 to 1482, imposed by his uncle Philip the Good of Burgundy. His rule provoked repeated risings, which ended with Charles the Bold's sack of Liège in 1468 and a Burgundian protectorate.

louis-of-burgundy.s: Louis of Burgundy was a younger son of Duke Robert II of Burgundy who married Matilda of Hainaut and became prince of Achaea in 1313. He defeated and killed his rival Ferdinand of Majorca at the Battle of Manolada in 1316, but died shortly after, reportedly of poison.

lgt-group.s: LGT is a private banking and asset management group owned by the princely family of Liechtenstein, which took over the Bank in Liechtenstein founded in 1920. In 2008 data stolen from its trust subsidiary exposed German tax evaders, causing a diplomatic dispute and…

liechtenstein-castle.s: Liechtenstein Castle stands near Maria Enzersdorf, south of Vienna, in Lower Austria. Built in the twelfth century, it gave its name to the Liechtenstein family, who lost it in the late Middle Ages and recovered it in 1807; the present castle was largely rebuilt in the…

latcu-of-moldavia.s: Lațcu was prince of Moldavia from about 1367 to about 1375, the son of Bogdan I. He sought a Catholic bishopric at Siret, established around 1371, to win papal support against Hungary.

lifan-yuan.s: The Lifan Yuan, or Court of Colonial Affairs, was the Qing government office that managed relations with Mongolia, Tibet, Xinjiang and other Inner Asian dependencies. Founded in 1638 from the Mongol Office of the Manchu state, it supervised the Mongol nobility and banners,…

luis-garcia-meza.s: Luis García Meza was a Bolivian general who seized power in the 'cocaine coup' of 17 July 1980, preventing the inauguration of the elected Hernán Siles Zuazo. His regime was marked by severe repression, the killing of opposition leaders and links with drug traffickers, and he…

la-higuera.s: La Higuera is a small village in the Vallegrande Province of the Santa Cruz Department, in the eastern Andean foothills of Bolivia. Che Guevara was held in its schoolhouse after his capture by the Bolivian army in October 1967 and executed there on 9 October.

luis-arce.s: Luis Arce is a Bolivian economist and politician who was minister of economy under Evo Morales for most of 2006–2019 and president of Bolivia from 2020 to 2025 for the Movement for Socialism (MAS). His presidency faced falling natural gas output, shortages of fuel and dollars,…

liberating-expedition-of-peru.s: The Liberating Expedition of Peru was the military campaign led by José de San Martín from Chile against the royalist stronghold of Peru. Carried by a Chilean fleet under Thomas Cochrane, it sailed from Valparaíso in August 1820 and landed near Pisco.

lai-ching-te.s: Lai Ching-te is a Taiwanese politician of the Democratic Progressive Party, a former physician who served as mayor of Tainan, premier and vice-president. He won the presidential election of January 2024 and took office as president of the Republic of China in May 2024, the…

land-to-the-tiller-act.s: The Land-to-the-Tiller programme of 1953 was the final stage of land reform in Taiwan under the Republic of China. Landlords were required to sell land above a fixed limit to the state, receiving compensation in commodity bonds and shares in state enterprises, and the land was…

lee-teng-hui.s: Lee Teng-hui was the first Taiwan-born president of the Republic of China, succeeding Chiang Ching-kuo in 1988 and serving until 2000. An agricultural economist, he led the transition to democracy, abolishing the Temporary Provisions in 1991, holding fully elected legislatures…

liberal-revolution-of-1895.s: The Liberal Revolution of 1895 in Ecuador began with a rising in Guayaquil on 5 June 1895 that proclaimed Eloy Alfaro supreme chief. Liberal forces then fought their way into the Sierra and took Quito, ending the conservative order.

liberal-revolution-of-1871.s: The Liberal Revolution of 1871 in Guatemala was the revolt led by Miguel García Granados and Justo Rufino Barrios that overthrew the conservative government of Vicente Cerna and entered Guatemala City on 30 June 1871. The liberal regimes that followed expelled the Jesuits,…

loja-ecuador.s: Loja is a city in the southern highlands of Ecuador, the capital of the province of the same name. Founded by the Spanish around 1548, it was a centre for the gold mining and cinchona bark trade of the region.

loja-spain.s: Loja is a town in the province of Granada in southern Spain, on the Genil River west of the city of Granada. A fortress of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada guarding the western approach to its capital, it resisted a Castilian siege in 1482 but was taken by Ferdinand and Isabella…

la-matanza.s: La Matanza, 'the massacre', was the killing of thousands of peasants, most of them indigenous Pipil, by the Salvadoran army and militias after an uprising in the coffee-growing west of El Salvador in January 1932. Estimates of the dead range from about 10,000 to over 30,000.

lennart-meri.s: Lennart Meri was an Estonian writer and film-maker who became the country's first president after the restoration of independence, serving from 1992 to 2001. Deported to Siberia as a child, he later wrote and filmed on the Finno-Ugric peoples.

lapland-finland.s: Lapland is the northernmost region of Finland, covering nearly a third of the country's area but home to fewer than 200,000 people, with Rovaniemi as its capital. Long inhabited by the Sámi, it is a land of forest, fells and tundra largely north of the Arctic Circle.

lapland-war.s: The Lapland War was fought between Finland and Germany in northern Finland from September 1944 to April 1945. Under its armistice with the Soviet Union, Finland had to expel the German forces stationed in Lapland; the Germans withdrew to Norway, destroying Rovaniemi and much…

lapua-movement.s: The Lapua Movement was a Finnish radical nationalist and anti-communist movement founded in the town of Lapua in Ostrobothnia in late 1929. It pressed the government into banning communist activity and kidnapped opponents, among them the former president K.

lex-kallio.s: Lex Kallio was a Finnish land law of 1922, named after the Agrarian politician Kyösti Kallio, that allowed the state to buy land and redistribute it to tenant farmers, crofters and landless rural workers. Building on the tenant-farmer law of 1918, it helped create tens of…

linus-torvalds.s: Linus Torvalds (born 1969) is a Finnish-American software engineer who created the Linux kernel in 1991 while a student at the University of Helsinki. Released as free software, Linux grew through the work of thousands of volunteers and companies into the basis of most web…

linux.s: Linux is a family of free and open-source operating systems built on the Linux kernel, first released in 1991 by the Finnish student Linus Torvalds. Developed collaboratively over the internet and usually combined with GNU software, it became the dominant system on web servers…

leonardo-bruni.s: Leonardo Bruni (c. 1370–1444) was an Italian humanist and historian who served as chancellor of Florence in 1410–1411 and again from 1427 until his death.

ligurian-republic.s: The Ligurian Republic was a French client state that replaced the aristocratic Republic of Genoa in 1797, after Napoleon Bonaparte pressed the old regime to give way to a democratic government. It covered Genoa and the Ligurian coast and was closely tied to France in the wars…

lamba-doria.s: Lamba Doria (1245–1323) was a Genoese admiral and statesman of the powerful Doria family. In 1298 he commanded the Genoese fleet that destroyed a Venetian fleet at the Battle of Curzola in the Adriatic, the greatest Genoese naval victory over its rival.

lanzarotto-malocello.s: Lanzarotto Malocello was a Genoese navigator who reached the Canary Islands in the early fourteenth century, traditionally around 1312, the first recorded European visit since antiquity. He is said to have lived for years on the island that bears his name, Lanzarote, which…

la-linea-case.s: La Línea was a customs fraud network in Guatemala in which officials took bribes from importers in exchange for lower duties, exposed in April 2015 by the International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala and the public prosecutor's office. The scandal led to mass…

louis-jean-jacques-acaau.s: Louis Jean-Jacques Acaau (died 1846) was a Haitian peasant leader and former army officer who led the piquets, an uprising of black smallholders in southern Haiti, in 1844. Demanding land, cheaper imported goods and justice for the poor against the mixed-race elite, the revolt…

lycee-petion.s: The Lycée Pétion is a secondary school in Port-au-Prince, founded in 1816 under President Alexandre Pétion and named after him. One of the oldest schools in Haiti and long the capital's leading public secondary school, it educated much of the country's political and…

la-ceiba.s: La Ceiba is a port city on the Caribbean coast of northern Honduras and capital of the department of Atlántida. It grew from the late nineteenth century as the base of the Vaccaro brothers' banana business, later the Standard Fruit Company, whose railways and docks made it one…

lenca-people.s: The Lenca are an indigenous people of western Honduras and eastern El Salvador, living mainly in the highland departments of Intibucá, Lempira and La Paz in Honduras. Their language died out in the twentieth century, but they keep distinctive traditions of pottery and ritual.

liberal-party-of-honduras.s: The Liberal Party of Honduras is one of the country's two traditional parties, founded in 1891 under Policarpo Bonilla. It alternated in power with the National Party through much of the twentieth century and, after the return to civilian rule in 1982, produced presidents…

liberal-party-of-australia.s: The Liberal Party of Australia is the country's main centre-right party, founded in 1944–1945 by Robert Menzies from the United Australia Party and other non-Labor groups. In a long-standing coalition with the Country, later National, Party, it governed from 1949 to 1972, with…

liberal-party-uk.s: The Liberal Party was one of the two major parties of the United Kingdom from its formation in 1859, out of the Whigs, Radicals and Peelites, until the First World War. Under William Gladstone and later H.

la-mosquitia.s: La Mosquitia is a sparsely populated region of rainforest, pine savanna and lagoons in eastern Honduras, the Honduran part of the Mosquito Coast that extends into Nicaragua. It is the homeland of the Miskito and other indigenous peoples, and from the seventeenth to the…

lal-bahadur-shastri.s: Lal Bahadur Shastri (1904–1966) was an Indian independence activist and Congress politician who succeeded Jawaharlal Nehru as prime minister in 1964. He led India in the war of 1965 with Pakistan and promoted food self-sufficiency with the slogan 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' (Hail…

lacplesis-day.s: Lāčplēsis Day is a Latvian day of remembrance held on 11 November for those who fell fighting for the country's independence. It commemorates the defeat of Pavel Bermondt-Avalov's West Russian Volunteer Army at Riga in November 1919 and takes its name from Lāčplēsis, the…

latvian-legion.s: The Latvian Legion was a formation of the Waffen-SS created in 1943 under German occupation, made up mainly of Latvian conscripts in the 15th and 19th Waffen Grenadier Divisions. It fought the Red Army on the Eastern Front, and the 19th Division held out in the Courland Pocket…

latvian-socialist-soviet-republic.s: The Latvian Socialist Soviet Republic was a Bolshevik state proclaimed in December 1918 under Pēteris Stučka and backed by the Red Army, which took Riga in January 1919. Its rule brought revolutionary tribunals, requisitions and famine in the capital.

lithuanian-nationalist-union.s: The Lithuanian Nationalist Union (Tautininkai) was a nationalist political party founded in 1924, led by Antanas Smetona and Augustinas Voldemaras. After the military coup of December 1926 it became the ruling party of Smetona's authoritarian regime and from the mid-1930s the…

lithuanian-byelorussian-soviet-socialist.s: The Lithuanian–Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, known as Litbel, was a short-lived Bolshevik state formed in February 1919 by merging the Soviet republics of Lithuania and Byelorussia, with its capital at Vilnius. It depended on the Red Army and collapsed when Polish…

lithuanian-riflemens-union.s: The Lithuanian Riflemen's Union is a paramilitary volunteer organisation founded in 1919 by Vladas Putvinskis to support the army during the wars of independence. Between the wars it grew into a mass organisation and took part in the seizure of Klaipėda in 1923; it was banned…

luis-somoza-debayle.s: Luis Somoza Debayle was president of Nicaragua from 1956 to 1963, succeeding his father, Anastasio Somoza García, after his assassination. More moderate than his father or his brother, he allowed limited reforms and handed the presidency to allies in 1963, while his brother…

luis-sanchez-cerro.s: Luis Sánchez Cerro was a Peruvian army officer who overthrew Augusto B. Leguía in August 1930 and, after a brief exile, won the disputed presidential election of 1931 against Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre.

lastovo.s: Lastovo is an island in the southern Adriatic, part of Croatia, lying about 80 kilometres west of Dubrovnik. It came under the Republic of Ragusa in the thirteenth century and kept its own statute and a degree of self-government until the republic's fall.

las-anod.s: Las Anod is a city in northern Somalia, the capital of the Sool region and the main town of the Dhulbahante clan. Contested between Somaliland and Puntland, it was taken by Somaliland forces in 2007.

lido-di-venezia.s: The Lido di Venezia is a long, narrow barrier island separating the Venetian lagoon from the Adriatic Sea. Its port entrance, the Bocca di Lido, was guarded by forts, and in April 1797 the firing on a French ship there gave Napoleon a pretext to declare war on the republic.

laocoon-and-his-sons.s: Laocoön and His Sons is a marble sculpture showing the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons attacked by sea serpents. Pliny the Elder attributed it to the Rhodian sculptors Hagesander, Athenodorus and Polydorus.

lex-rhodia.s: The Lex Rhodia was the maritime law of Rhodes on jettison: when cargo was thrown overboard to save a ship, the loss was shared among all whose property had been saved. Roman jurists adopted the rule, and it appears in Justinian's Digest.

legio-ix-hispana.s: Legio IX Hispana was a Roman legion that took part in the invasion of Britain in 43 CE. It was badly defeated by Boudica's rebels in 60 or 61 and later built the legionary fortress at York.

legio-xiv-gemina.s: Legio XIV Gemina was a legion of the Roman army and one of the four that took part in the emperor Claudius's invasion of Britain in 43 CE. It played a leading part in Suetonius Paulinus's defeat of Boudica's revolt in 60 or 61, earning the title Martia Victrix, and was later…

life-of-antony.s: The Life of Antony is a biography of the Egyptian hermit Anthony the Great, written in Greek by Athanasius of Alexandria soon after Anthony's death in 356. It describes his withdrawal into the desert, his struggles with demons and his holiness.

legio-ii-traiana-fortis.s: Legio II Traiana Fortis was a Roman legion raised by the emperor Trajan around 105 CE. From the reign of Hadrian it was stationed at Nicopolis near Alexandria, and for most of the second and third centuries it was the only legion in Egypt.

lucius-junius-brutus.s: Lucius Junius Brutus was the legendary founder of the Roman Republic. According to Roman tradition he led the revolt that expelled the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, in 509 BCE and became one of the first two consuls.

lex-hortensia.s: The Lex Hortensia was a Roman law of 287 BCE, passed under the dictator Quintus Hortensius after a secession of the plebeians. It made the resolutions of the plebeian assembly binding on all Roman citizens, patricians included.

lex-villia-annalis.s: The Lex Villia Annalis was a Roman law of 180 BCE, proposed by the tribune Lucius Villius. It set minimum ages for holding the senior magistracies and required an interval between offices, fixing the order of the cursus honorum, the ladder of public offices in the Roman Republic.

livius-andronicus.s: Livius Andronicus was a Greek from Tarentum who became the first known Latin poet and dramatist. Brought to Rome probably as a captive, he translated Homer's Odyssey into Latin verse, and in 240 BCE he staged the first Latin play adapted from a Greek original.

lucretius.s: Lucretius, in full Titus Lucretius Carus, was a Roman poet and philosopher of the first century BCE. His poem On the Nature of Things (De rerum natura) set out the physics and ethics of Epicurus, arguing that the universe consists of atoms and void and that fear of the gods…

limigantes.s: The Limigantes were a subject people of the Sarmatians on the middle Danube in the fourth century CE, ruled by a dominant group the Romans called the Argaragantes. In 334 they rose against their masters and drove them out, and many of the refugees were settled in the Roman…

legio-iii-gallica.s: Legio III Gallica was a Roman legion probably raised by Julius Caesar around 49 BCE. It served in Mark Antony's Parthian campaign and was long stationed in Syria; moved to Moesia in 68 CE, it destroyed a raiding force of some 9,000 Roxolani horsemen there early in 69 before…

lebuin.s: Lebuin was an English monk and missionary who worked in the eastern Netherlands in the mid-eighth century, founding a church at Deventer. According to his Life, he went to the annual Saxon assembly at Marklo on the Weser to preach and narrowly escaped death.

lex-saxonum.s: The Lex Saxonum is the law code of the Saxons, written down in Latin under Charlemagne, probably in connection with the assembly of Aachen in 802–803. It combined Saxon customary law with Frankish additions and set graded compensation payments that valued nobles far above…

layla-and-majnun.s: Layla and Majnun is a Persian narrative poem by Nizami Ganjavi, completed in 1188 at the request of the Shirvanshah Akhsitan I. Based on an Arabic tale of the poet Qays, driven mad by his hopeless love for Layla, it became one of the best-known love stories of the Islamic world.

lal-singh.s: Lal Singh was a courtier of the Sikh Empire, a favourite of the regent Maharani Jind Kaur, who became wazir (chief minister) in 1845. He commanded Sikh troops in the First Anglo-Sikh War and was widely accused of betraying them to the British.

lang-son.s: Lạng Sơn is a city and province in north-eastern Vietnam on the main road and railway to China, near the Friendship Pass border crossing. For centuries it guarded the route of invasions from the north.

le-kha-phieu.s: Le Kha Phieu was a Vietnamese army officer and politician who served as general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam from 1997 to 2001. A former political commissar in the army, he was seen as cautious about economic reform, and his term saw the land border treaty with…

ladysmith-kwazulu-natal.s: Ladysmith is a town in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, on the Klip River, founded in 1850 and named after Juana María, the Spanish-born wife of the Cape governor Sir Harry Smith. In the Second Boer War, Boer forces besieged the British garrison there for 118 days, from November…

london-convention-1884.s: The London Convention was an agreement signed on 27 February 1884 between Britain and a Transvaal delegation led by Paul Kruger. It replaced the Pretoria Convention of 1881, restored the name South African Republic, redrew its western border and dropped any mention of British…

leonid-brezhnev.s: Leonid Brezhnev led the Soviet Union as first secretary, later general secretary, of the Communist Party from 1964 until his death in 1982. His long rule brought stability for officials, a military build-up to nuclear parity with the United States and détente in the 1970s, but…

leotychidas-ii.s: Leotychidas II was a Eurypontid king of Sparta who gained the throne about 491 BCE after Cleomenes I had his rival Demaratus deposed. In 479 BCE he commanded the Greek fleet and army that destroyed the Persian forces at Mycale in Ionia.

life-of-lycurgus.s: The Life of Lycurgus is a biography of the legendary Spartan lawgiver by the Greek writer Plutarch, part of his Parallel Lives, where it is paired with the life of the Roman king Numa. It describes the Spartan constitution, the redistribution of land, the common meals and the…

lord-chunshen.s: Lord Chunshen, personal name Huang Xie, was chief minister of the State of Chu for about twenty-five years under King Kaolie, and one of the Four Lords of the Warring States, famous for keeping thousands of retainers. He led Chu forces to relieve Handan in 257 BCE and…

li-sao.s: The Li Sao (Encountering Sorrow) is a long poem of about 370 lines attributed to Qu Yuan, minister of the State of Chu in the late fourth century BCE, and the opening work of the Chu Ci anthology. In it a loyal noble slandered at court laments his fate and makes a visionary…

li-xin-qin.s: Li Xin was a general of the State of Qin during its wars of unification. He pursued the crown prince of Yan, Dan, after the attempt on the life of the future First Emperor, and in 225 BCE led a Qin army of about 200,000 men against Chu, which was routed by the Chu general…

li-county-gansu.s: Li County, or Lixian, is a county in Longnan in south-eastern Gansu, China, in the upper valley of the Western Han River. Excavations there, including large tombs at Dabuzishan attributed to early Qin rulers, show that a Qin elite was established in the area by the eighth…

liye.s: Liye is a town in Longshan County, western Hunan, China. In 2002 excavators found a well at an ancient walled site there containing tens of thousands of inscribed wooden slips from the archive of the Qin county of Qianling, dating from about 222 to 208 BCE.

loe-thai.s: Loe Thai was king of Sukhothai in the early fourteenth century, the son and successor of Ram Khamhaeng. During his reign many of the distant dependencies gathered by his father broke away, and the kingdom shrank to its core around the Yom and Nan valleys.

lake-beysehir.s: Lake Beyşehir is a large freshwater lake in south-western Turkey, in the provinces of Konya and Isparta, and the largest freshwater lake in the country. The Seljuk sultan Kayqubad I built the palace of Kubadabad on its shore in the 1230s, and the town of Beyşehir at its…

lloyd-mathews.s: Sir Lloyd Mathews was a British naval officer who in 1877 entered the service of Sultan Barghash of Zanzibar to raise a regular army trained on European lines, which grew to more than a thousand men. After Zanzibar became a British protectorate in 1890 he served as the…

lalla-rookh-ship.s: The Lalla Rookh was the sailing ship that brought the first indentured labourers from British India to Suriname, arriving at Paramaribo on 5 June 1873 with about four hundred passengers. Their arrival began the migration of some 34,000 Indians to the colony up to 1916, the…

lokono.s: The Lokono, often called Arawaks, are an Indigenous people of the coastal Guianas who speak an Arawakan language. They traded and fought with European colonists in the seventeenth century, and in 1686 Governor Van Aerssen of Suriname made peace with them and the Kalina.

labotsibeni-mdluli.s: Labotsibeni Mdluli was queen mother of Swaziland, mother of Ngwane V and grandmother of Sobhuza II. She acted as regent during her son's minority and, after his death in 1899, governed for her grandson until 1921.

libandla.s: The Libandla is the general national council of the Swazi, an assembly of chiefs, councillors and other men that the king traditionally consulted on matters affecting the nation. Its name is also used for the modern Parliament of Eswatini.

liqoqo.s: The Liqoqo is the inner council of senior princes, chiefs and advisers that counsels the king of Eswatini. After the death of Sobhuza II in 1982 it became the dominant power in the kingdom during the regency and was involved in a bitter struggle at court, until the young…

lobamba.s: Lobamba is the traditional, royal and legislative capital of Eswatini, in the Ezulwini valley between Mbabane and Manzini. It is the seat of the queen mother and the Parliament, and the site of the Incwala and Umhlanga ceremonies, the national museum and the memorial of…

lydenburg.s: Lydenburg is a town in Mpumalanga, South Africa, founded in 1849 by Voortrekkers who left nearby Ohrigstad because of malaria. It was the capital of the small Lydenburg Republic from 1856 until it joined the South African Republic in 1860.

landammann-of-switzerland.s: The Landammann of Switzerland was the head of the Swiss Confederation under Napoleon's Act of Mediation from 1803 to 1813. The office rotated each year with the seat of the federal Diet among six directorial cantons, Fribourg, Bern, Solothurn, Basel, Zurich and Lucerne, and…

long-diet.s: The Long Diet was the assembly of the Swiss cantons that sat in Zurich from April 1814 to August 1815, after the fall of the Napoleonic order. Its long negotiations produced the Federal Treaty, sworn on 7 August 1815, which bound twenty-two cantons, including the newly…

li-yuanji.s: Li Yuanji was the fourth son of Li Yuan, founder of the Tang dynasty, and held the title Prince of Qi. He sided with the crown prince Li Jiancheng against their brother Li Shimin, and both were killed by Li Shimin's men in the Xuanwu Gate Incident of 626.

leopoldo-batres.s: Leopoldo Batres was a Mexican archaeologist who served as inspector of archaeological monuments under Porfirio Díaz. He led the first large-scale excavation and reconstruction of the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan, completed for the centenary of Mexican independence in 1910.

lhalung-palgyi-dorje.s: Lhalung Palgyi Dorje was a ninth-century Tibetan Buddhist monk who, according to later Buddhist histories, assassinated the emperor Langdarma with an arrow, traditionally in 842, to end his persecution of Buddhism. The story, which modern historians treat with caution, became…

langdarma.s: Langdarma, also called Udumtsen, was the last emperor of a united Tibet, succeeding his murdered brother Ralpachen in 838. Later Buddhist histories portray him as a persecutor of Buddhism assassinated by the monk Lhalung Palgyi Dorje, traditionally in 842; modern historians…

lake-palace.s: The Lake Palace is a palace on Jag Niwas island in Lake Pichola at Udaipur, built in 1743–1746 by Maharana Jagat Singh II of Mewar as a summer residence. Its white marble buildings appear to float on the water.

lake-pichola.s: Lake Pichola is an artificial lake at Udaipur in Rajasthan, created according to tradition in 1362 when a Banjara grain trader dammed a stream. Udai Singh II enlarged it after founding Udaipur on its eastern shore in 1559, and its islands and banks hold the City Palace, Jag…

lords-resistance-army.s: The Lord's Resistance Army is a rebel group founded in northern Uganda in 1987 by Joseph Kony, who claimed spiritual guidance and declared the aim of ruling by the Ten Commandments. Drawing on the Acholi insurgency against Yoweri Museveni's government, it waged a war of…

luwero-triangle.s: The Luwero Triangle is an area of central Uganda north of Kampala, centred on the Luweero district of Buganda. It was the main battleground of the Bush War of 1981–1986 between Milton Obote's government and Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army, and counter-insurgency…

louvre-abu-dhabi.s: The Louvre Abu Dhabi is an art and civilisation museum on Saadiyat Island in Abu Dhabi, opened in November 2017 under a 2007 agreement between the United Arab Emirates and France that lent it the Louvre's name. Designed by Jean Nouvel beneath a vast perforated dome, it…

luftwaffe.s: The Luftwaffe was the air force of Nazi Germany, unveiled in 1935 in defiance of the Treaty of Versailles and commanded by Hermann Göring. It supported the Blitzkrieg campaigns of 1939–1941 but was defeated in the Battle of Britain and worn down by Allied air power by 1944;…

landlord-and-tenant-ireland-act-1870.s: The Landlord and Tenant (Ireland) Act 1870, Gladstone's first Irish Land Act, sought to protect Irish tenant farmers. It gave legal force to the Ulster custom of tenant right where it existed, entitled evicted tenants to compensation for improvements and offered loans for…

liverpool-and-manchester-railway.s: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, opened in September 1830, was the first inter-city railway in the world to rely entirely on steam locomotives and to carry both passengers and freight on a timetable. Built with George Stephenson as engineer and known for the Rainhill…

lok-sabha.s: The Lok Sabha, or House of the People, is the lower house of the Parliament of India, first constituted in 1952 after the country's first general election. Its members are elected by universal adult suffrage from single-member constituencies, and the prime minister and council…

lewis-and-clark-expedition.s: The Lewis and Clark Expedition was a United States Army expedition led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark from 1804 to 1806 to explore the newly acquired Louisiana Purchase and find a route to the Pacific. Aided by the Shoshone woman Sacagawea, it travelled up the Missouri…

lugal-kinishe-dudu.s: Lugal-kinishe-dudu was a king of Uruk in the Early Dynastic period, around the twenty-fourth century BCE, who also ruled Ur and claimed kingship over both cities. Inscriptions of Enmetena of Lagash record a pact of brotherhood with him, one of the earliest known diplomatic…

lake-maracaibo.s: Lake Maracaibo is a large brackish tidal bay, usually called a lake, in north-western Venezuela, joined to the Gulf of Venezuela by a narrow strait. The basin beneath it holds some of the world's largest oil deposits; the blowout of the Barroso II well at Cabimas in 1922…

laurentian-codex.s: The Laurentian Codex is a Russian manuscript copied in 1377 by the monk Lavrenty for Prince Dmitry Konstantinovich of Suzdal and Nizhny Novgorod. It contains the oldest surviving copy of the Primary Chronicle, followed by a continuation based on the chronicles of…

laoshang-chanyu.s: Laoshang was chanyu of the Xiongnu from 174 to 161 BCE, the son and successor of Modu. He completed the defeat of the Yuezhi, killing their king and, according to Chinese sources, making his skull into a drinking cup, which drove the Yuezhi westwards.

linear-a.s: Linear A is the undeciphered script used by the Minoans of Crete for administration and religious inscriptions from about 1800 to 1450 BCE. Written on clay tablets, sealings and stone vessels, it records an unknown language.

linear-b.s: Linear B is the syllabic script used by the Mycenaean palaces of Greece and Crete from about 1450 to 1200 BCE to record an early form of Greek. Adapted from Linear A, it survives on clay tablets from Knossos, Pylos, Mycenae, Thebes and other sites, listing goods, workers, land…

lordship-of-rappoltstein.s: The Lordship of Rappoltstein (Ribeaupierre) was a territory in Upper Alsace centred on Ribeauvillé, held by the lords of Rappoltstein from the Middle Ages, whose three castles stand above the town. When the family died out in 1673, it passed by marriage to Christian II of…

la-petite-pierre.s: La Petite-Pierre (German Lützelstein) is a small town in the northern Vosges in Alsace, France, dominated by a castle on a sandstone ridge. Seat of the counts of Lützelstein in the Middle Ages, it passed to the Palatine Wittelsbachs and was a residence of the…

leopold-louis-count-palatine-of-veldenz.n: Leopold Louis, Count Palatine of Veldenz
leopold-louis-count-palatine-of-veldenz.s: Leopold Louis was the last Count Palatine of Veldenz, ruling the small principality from 1634 to 1694. His lands suffered in the Thirty Years' War and the French wars of Louis XIV.

longinus-missionary.s: Longinus was a Miaphysite bishop and missionary who worked in Nubia in the 6th century. Consecrated bishop for the kingdom of Nobadia in the 560s, he spent several years organising its church, and around 580 he travelled south to the kingdom of Alodia, whose king and court he…

lakshmana-temple-sirpur.s: The Lakshmana Temple at Sirpur in Chhattisgarh, India, is a brick temple of the 7th century dedicated to Vishnu, built by Queen Vasata, mother of the Panduvamshi king Mahashivagupta Balarjuna. Its tower and finely carved doorframe make it one of the best-preserved examples of…

lakshmana-temple-khajuraho.s: The Lakshmana Temple is a Hindu temple at Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh, India, dedicated to Vishnu and completed around 954 under the Chandela kings Yashovarman and Dhanga. Standing on a high platform with four subsidiary shrines at its corners, it is one of the earliest and…

lucius-caecilius-metellus-consul-251-bce.s: Lucius Caecilius Metellus was a Roman commander of the First Punic War, consul in 251 and 247 BCE. In 250 BCE, as proconsul, he defeated the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal outside Panormus in Sicily, throwing his war elephants into confusion with missiles and capturing many of…

louis-auguste-blanqui.s: Louis Auguste Blanqui was a French revolutionary socialist who spent more than thirty years of his life in prison. He held that a small, disciplined group of conspirators should seize power and set up a temporary dictatorship on behalf of the people, a doctrine known as…
